output:
Sunlight looks white, but it is not a single colour. It is every colour mixed together, which you can see for yourself whenever a rainbow appears. A prism or a raindrop simply pulls that mixture apart again.

Each colour travels as a wave, and the waves are not the same size. Red light has long, lazy waves. Blue and violet light have short, tight ones. That difference in size is what decides the colour of your sky.

Earth's air is full of gas molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen, far too small to see. When sunlight streams through, these molecules knock the light sideways. Scattering, it is called. The catch is that they are much better at knocking short waves around than long ones. Blue gets bounced in all directions; red mostly sails straight past.

So when you look up at an empty patch of sky, you are seeing blue light that has been scattered off countless molecules and redirected down into your eyes. The sun itself still looks yellowish because it has lost some of its blue along the way.

Sunsets flip the picture. With the sun low, its light cuts through far more air, and nearly all the blue scatters away long before it reaches you. What survives the journey is red and orange.

In short, the sky is blue because air scatters short blue waves more strongly than any other colour.
